title: Cut Vertices, Bridges and Blocks
quickIdea: A cut vertex or a bridge is a single point of failure, and two DFS rules find all of them in linear time; a bridge is exactly an edge that lies on no cycle.
remember: v is a cut vertex (articulation point) when G - v has more components than G; e is a bridge when G - e does.
An edge is a bridge if and only if it lies on no simple cycle, so every edge of a tree is a bridge and no edge of a cycle is.

In a connected graph on n at least 3 vertices the endpoints of a bridge are cut vertices, so a cut edge forces a cut vertex; the converse fails, since two triangles sharing one vertex have a cut vertex and no bridge.
A connected graph on n vertices has at most n-2 cut vertices, reached by a path on n vertices.
DFS rule for the root: the root of a DFS tree is a cut vertex if and only if it has at least two children.
DFS rule for other vertices: v is a cut vertex if and only if some child subtree of v has no back edge to a proper ancestor of v, that is low[child] is at least disc[v].
A leaf of a DFS tree is never a cut vertex, and the biconnected components (blocks) of a graph share only cut vertices.

example.prompt: Take a triangle abc with a pendant edge cd hanging from c. List the cut vertices and the bridges.
example.work: Deleting c isolates d, so the graph splits and c is a cut vertex. Deleting a, b or d leaves the rest connected, so none of them is a cut vertex. Deleting edge cd isolates d, so cd is a bridge. Deleting ab, bc or ca leaves the triangle connected through its other two sides, so none of those three is a bridge.
example.answer: One cut vertex, c, and one bridge, cd.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2021 Set 1 Q.41 asked exactly the two DFS rules and GATE CSE 2015 Set 2 Q.50 asked the bridge-on-a-cycle fact. Both are definition questions worth marks per option, not coding questions.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A connected graph on 6 vertices has 5 edges. How many bridges does it have?
variations.answer: 5. A connected graph with n-1 edges is a tree, and every edge of a tree is a bridge.
variations.why: Connected plus n-1 edges forces a tree, and deleting any tree edge separates the tree into two parts.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Can a graph have a cut vertex but no bridge?
variations.answer: Yes. Two triangles sharing exactly one vertex: removing the shared vertex disconnects the graph, but no single edge does.
variations.why: Cut vertices are about vertices and bridges about edges; only the direction 'bridge implies cut vertex' holds, and only for n at least 3.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: In a DFS tree of a connected graph the root has one child, and every other vertex has a child subtree with a back edge to a proper ancestor. How many cut vertices does the graph have?
variations.answer: None. A root with one child is not a cut vertex, and every other vertex has a low value below its own discovery time, so none of them is a cut vertex either.
variations.why: Both DFS rules must fail for a vertex to be safe; here both do.

trap.what: Saying 'a cut edge always gives a cut vertex' without the n at least 3 condition, and calling a leaf of a DFS tree a cut vertex.
trap.why: In K_2, removing either endpoint leaves a single vertex, which is connected, so the bridge has no cut vertex at all. A DFS leaf has no descendant to be cut off from the rest.
trap.counterexample: K_2 has a bridge and no cut vertex; in the triangle with pendant edge cd, the pendant vertex d is a leaf of a DFS tree rooted at a and is not a cut vertex.

check.question: A cycle C_6 has one chord joining two opposite vertices. How many cut vertices does the resulting graph have?
check.explanation: The chord splits C_6 into two cycles of length 4 that share only the chord's endpoints, and each of those endpoints still has two independent routes into the other cycle. Removing any vertex leaves a path plus a chord, which stays connected, so no vertex is a cut vertex; scripts/validate.py checks this by removing each vertex in turn.

sources.note: slide text read through graph basics, walk/path/circuit, Euler and Hamiltonian, cut-set and cut-vertex, edge and vertex connectivity, colouring, bipartite, independent set, matching and Hall's theorem; the fetch was truncated after the Havel-Hakimi example, so the later matching pages were read only as excerpts

sourceLine: Cut vertices, bridges, the DFS rules and biconnected components: GATE Overflow GO Classroom deck (English, read in part) for the cut-set, cut-vertex and edge/vertex-connectivity definitions; CLRS ch. 22 problem 22-2 for the two DFS rules. Standard references used to verify, never copied: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications, ch. 10; West, Introduction to Graph Theory (Brooks, Dirac, Koenig, chromatic polynomial); CLRS ch. 22 (articulation points, bridges) and ch. 26 (bipartite matching); Diestel, Graph Theory (Menger). The bridge-on-a-cycle equivalence, the n-2 bound and the DFS rules are all recomputed in scripts/validate.py over every graph on up to 5 vertices.
